overview: This imported Arakan outline covers 200 BCE to 200 CE. It does not establish a kingdom lasting exactly those years. The better-documented cities and inscriptions discussed below are mostly later; their rulers and customs should not be moved backward into this early interval.

periods.title: An uncertain early map interval
periods.summary: Political dates are not established by this outline.

sections.title: What the early label can and cannot tell us

items.text: Dhanyawadi is a real archaeological site, but its starting date remains unevenly reported. Mya Oo’s historical introduction mentions evidence from the first century CE; archaeologist Elisabeth Moore generally dates the city from the fourth to sixth centuries. Neither source establishes this map’s 200 BCE beginning.
The imported polygon includes Dhanyawadi but leaves Vesali beyond its southeastern edge, judging from published site coordinates. Its boundary should not be read as an exact ancient frontier.

The later Anandacandra pillar looks far back into the past. Its early royal list includes extraordinarily long reigns, and Johnston regarded that opening sequence as at least partly mythical. Such a royal account tells us how a later court imagined its ancestry; it cannot independently certify centuries of earlier kings.

We have not verified a written-language sample securely belonging to this record’s 200 BCE to 200 CE span. The Sanskrit and Pali inscriptions central to studies of early Arakan belong to later contexts. Printing one of those without its date would give this early map a misleading voice.

sections.title: Discoveries that clarify the later landscape

items.text: Modern fieldwork corrected Dhanyawadi’s archaeological plan: earth banks once drawn as part of an oddly shaped city wall proved to be a separate feature. Brickwork underneath helped reveal the older wall’s course. This is a lesson in checking maps on the ground; it does not date those walls to 200 BCE.

For the much later Vesali, excavators in 1980 to 1984 uncovered a monastery and a hall interpreted as a place for monastic ordinations, measuring 21 by 15 meters. Such buildings show organized religious communities. Their existence should not become a claim that children in this earlier map interval attended the same institutions.

Household meals, family routines, remedies and toilets cannot be reconstructed for this exact early interval from the sources checked here. Later inscriptions illuminate donors and religious institutions far better than ordinary homes. Leaving those gaps visible is preferable to giving an ancient family a menu borrowed from people living centuries afterward.

The famous pillar now at Mrauk U carries writing from several later periods on different faces. Much is worn away. Its present location is also later than its inscriptions: local history says a sixteenth-century king moved it from Vesali. An artifact can have a long traveling life, quite apart from the story written on it.

ending.text: The year 200 CE is the end of this map fragment, not a demonstrated conquest or disappearance. Later cities developed in the region, but the evidence checked here does not supply an uninterrupted sequence of rulers connecting this early outline to them.
